title: Author's purpose and audience
official_expectation: Determine the purpose (e.g., entertain, inform, persuade) and target audience of a text.
instructional_goal: Every author writes for a reason and for someone: to inform, to persuade or to entertain, and for a certain reader.
explicit_teaching: To inform means to teach facts. The text tells you true things about a topic. | To persuade means to get you to do something or to agree. Look for words like should and let's, and for reasons that try to change your mind. | Check what the whole text mostly does. Directions like "Bring a water bottle" or "Please come early" tell you how to do something. They inform; they are not trying to change your mind. | To entertain means to give you a fun story, a joke or a poem to enjoy. | The audience is who the text is for. Look for names, the word you, and what the reader is asked to know or do.
model_demands: What is the author's purpose, and who is the audience? | What is the author's purpose?

title: Text features: headings, bold words, text boxes and diagrams
official_expectation: Determine common text features of print, digital, auditory, spoken, and visual modes and describe how they contribute to the overall purpose and effect.
instructional_goal: Text features are the helpers around the paragraphs. They show you where to look and what is important.
explicit_teaching: A heading is a small title over a section. It tells what that section is about. | A bold word is printed in dark letters. Bold tells you, "This is a key word. Learn it." A bold word often names the big idea of its section, and the sentences around it tell what it means. You can also check its meaning in a glossary at the back. | A text box is set apart from the paragraphs. It often gives an extra fact, like a "Did You Know?" box. | A picture or photo shows what the words describe. The caption under it tells what the picture shows. A caption can also tell something the picture cannot show, like where or when. | A diagram is a drawing with labels. Each label has a line that points to one part and names it. A figure number, like Figure 1, helps you match a picture to the words about it. | Features are not only on paper. A web page has its own features. Menu tabs take you to other parts of the site. A search box finds pages when you type a word. A play button starts a video or a sound. A pop-up box tells what a word means without leaving the page. A link opens a new page with more facts. | Sound has features too. A caption line under a video shows in words what you would hear. Words in [brackets] name a sound, like [frog croaks]. A name and a colon, like NARRATOR:, shows who is talking. In a talk or a read-aloud, the speaker's voice does the job of bold print: a speaker may slow down, stop for a moment, or say "Listen closely" right before an important part.
model_demands: What does the heading tell you before you read the section? | Why is stem in bold, and what does it help you understand about the cactus? | How do the caption and the labels in Figure 1 help the reader?

guided_practice_prompts: Under which heading should you look to learn how beavers warn each other? | Which caption best fits the picture? | Why does the ranger say, "Listen closely. This next part is important"? | Choose the words that best complete the sentences.
independent_practice_prompts: How does the bold print help the reader? | Look at Figure 1. Which two sentences in the article tell about the parts that its labels point to? Choose two sentences. | Match each feature to the job it does. Three are in a printed book, and one is in a talk you listen to.
check_prompts: How does the text box add to the article? | Look at Figure 1 next to the section "From Egg to Wing." This question has two parts. Answer Part A, then Part B. | Choose the words that best complete the sentences. | What does the caption line tell the viewer? | What would the glossary most likely say about the bold word? | Look at Figure 2 and read its caption. title: When, where and why a text was written
official_expectation: With adult support, identify the context in which a text is written (e.g., time period, individual, situational).

title: How a text is put together: sections, patterns and features
official_expectation: Describe how texts are arranged to represent information and ideas using text features (e.g., map, captions) and organizational structures (e.g., cause/effect), referring to parts of texts using terms such as chapter or section.
instructional_goal: Authors build a text with a plan: headings split it into sections, a pattern links the ideas, and features like captions and maps help you understand.
explicit_teaching: Sequence tells steps or events in order. Look for clue words like first, next, then, after that, later and finally. | Cause and effect tells what happened and why. Look for because, so, since, as a result, that is why and this caused. | Compare tells how things are alike and different. Look for both, alike, same, but, however, unlike, different and while. | Problem and solution tells about a trouble and how it gets fixed. Look for problem, tried, but, decided, solved and finally. | Description tells about one topic with details. Look for for example, such as, also, in addition, has and looks like. Stories have clue words too: one day, but, then, so, finally and in the end. | Features help you understand. Headings split a text into sections and tell what each one is about. Captions tell what a picture shows, maps show where places are, and a text box sets apart an extra fact. In a book, the table of contents lists the chapters and the page where each one starts, so you know where to look.

title: Linking words: because, also, although, since and for example
official_expectation: Use conjunctions and transition words or phrases, such as although and since, to add cohesion and link ideas and information.

official_expectation: Identify and describe the use of figurative language, such as similes, metaphors, and idioms in a wide variety of texts.
instructional_goal: Authors use special language to help you picture things: a simile compares with like or as, a metaphor says one thing is another, and an idiom is a saying that means something different from its words.

"I like pizza" does not compare anything.

title: Use figurative language in your writing: similes, metaphors, idioms and more
official_expectation: Use figurative language, such as similes, metaphors, and idioms, to show relationships between ideas and information.
instructional_goal: You can make your writing come alive with figurative language: a simile with like or as, a metaphor that says one thing is another, an idiom, and more, as long as it fits what you mean.
explicit_teaching: First decide what you want your reader to picture or feel. Is it fast, loud, quiet, happy or scared? | Think of something that is very fast, loud or quiet. Then compare: "as quiet as a mouse." Make sure the comparison fits. A slow bus is "as slow as a turtle," not "as fast as a jet." | Use an idiom only when its meaning matches. "A piece of cake" means easy, so it fits an easy test, not a hard one. | A comparison shows how two ideas are alike. It helps your reader connect a new idea to one they already know. | Similes, metaphors and idioms are not the only kinds of figurative language. You can also give a thing a person's actions, like "The wind whispered through the trees." Use it only if it fits what you mean.
